# Parkikko: make your parking life easier\!

*Technical report  \|  Jamila Shulekha, Mai Phuong Pham, Ömer Furkan Tercan*

# Introduction

Have you ever been in your car, driving around while you try to find a parking spot, only to realise you might have missed the sign or it is shown in the other direction? There’s no need to worry anymore, because Parkikko helps you with finding the perfect parking spot for you. 

Parkikko is a mobile-friendly web application that tracks your location (with permission, of course\!) to find you the perfect parking spot nearby for you. When you are driving your car, it may be so that you see a free spot and want to park there, but the signs explain the duration you are allowed to park, the fee if you park for too long, and the hours within which free parking is allowed. Parkikko informs you about the place you are parked at: the fees, the free periods, and the possibility of being fined, and if so, by how much. It also may suggest nearby parking spots with the details if you do not manage to find a parking spot on your own. As well, it has a built-in alarm that will remind you ten to fifteen minutes before your parking period expires so you do not have to face fines. 

We planned to build a mobile-friendly web app UI/UX that would show the map of Helsinki for now and could be expanded to farther areas if needed in real life should it ever be picked up and developed into an actual working app. We managed to find open-source data from the City of Helsinki’s website, which has a map of all the street parking available, which is divided into various different subsections, which show if an area has free street parking or paid parking, the maximum duration of free parking, if it is prohibited to park somewhere after certain hours of the day, et cetera. 

# Data collection

The primary source is the [City of Helsinki Web Feature Service (WFS)](https://kartta.hel.fi/avoindata/dokumentit/Aineistolista_wms_avoindata.html), which contains 8,754 parking-area polygons, and avoindata:Piirijako\_peruspiiri, which supplies 34 basic districts. The pipeline requests metric coordinates (EPSG:3879), downloads paginated GeoJSON, and saves the server responses under data/raw/YYYY-MM-DD/. The data is published under CC BY 4.0 and does not require a login or API key.  
The holiday calendar is generated from the Python holidays package and exported as a small JSON file so the browser can apply holiday-specific parking windows without running Python. The calendar covers three years from generation; holidays and the preceding days can use different sign windows, and Christmas Eve and Midsummer Eve are flagged as uncertain parking holidays.

# Preprocessing

The main preprocessing task is to turn human-readable rules into fields the application can evaluate. pipeline/rules.py maps the city’s parking class and space type into paid, free\_limited, banned\_hours, always\_banned, reserved, or unknown. Space type can override the class: for example, a taxi bay is reserved even if its class would otherwise suggest paid parking. Unknown classes or space types become unknown rather than being assigned a plausible but unsupported label. 

Dedicated parsers normalize opening hours, durations, and seasons. For example, 9-21, (9-18) becomes Monday-Friday 09:00-21:00 and Saturday 09:00-18:00; the bracket convention and a third unbracketed range are used to identify weekend windows. The strings 4 h, 4h, 4 H and 4 are normalized to 240 minutes when they occur in the duration field; explicit “no time limit” is represented as zero, while an absent value remains missing. Seasonal date ranges are parsed into start and end dates. Plain sign-reference codes are retained as metadata, while prose conditions the parser cannot interpret are preserved for display to the driver. The most important design choice is fail-closed parsing. A parser must account for the entire field rather than silently accepting a recognizable substring. Thus 7-18 7-15 is ambiguous, and max 60 min lauantai is unreadable because the weekday condition would otherwise be lost. Each parking area receives a status, machine-readable issue code and plain-language reason. official means a complete rule was parsed; missing\_hours means the rule type is known but hours are absent for a rule that needs them; uncertain means the data is unreadable, ambiguous, or inconsistent. This distinction avoids treating missing data as a parsing error, or turning contradictory data into confident guidance.

Geospatial validation is equally important. The pipeline checks that identifiers are present and unique, geometries are non-empty polygons, and coordinate magnitudes are plausible for metric Helsinki coordinates. A GeoJSON file conventionally declares WGS84 even if its coordinates are actually metric; the pipeline explicitly assigns EPSG:3879 on read, checks the bounds, and converts to WGS84 only for the web export. District membership is assigned using each polygon’s centroid, avoiding dependence on row order for areas crossing boundaries. The web export keeps only fields the app needs, rounds coordinates to five decimals, and omits empty or null properties so absence has a consistent meaning.

We design the data model and add standardized rule fields and labels in English to easily manage and explore the data.

# Reflection and future work

While we’d initially planned to deliver a fully functioning web application page which could be interacted with to get an idea of the working app, it’s been a bit difficult to do so and, therefore, we present all the data that is needed to build the app in the above mentioned sections. For now, due to using the data that we acquired from the City of Helsinki’s website about street parking, the app is only in use for the city of Helsinki. Should developers want to work on it further, they can expand it to work beyond Helsinki’s borders. They can develop it to include Uusimaa or even all of Finland if they wanted.
